terms.gloss: a mole, a stone pier or breakwater
evidence: Caes. BC 1.25: mōlēs atque aggerem ab utrāque parte lītoris jaciēbat
terms.comment: Properly a great mass; of a harbour, the solid pier of stone and rubble thrown out into the sea, which is what a Roman pier was. Pliny calls the two moles of a harbour its arms (brachia). For a pier on piles, such as a seaside promenade, we have found no classical word; Morgan–Owens suggests, with a query, ambulācrum sublicium.

phrases.latin: Ambulēmus in mōle ūsque ad pharum.
phrases.english: Let’s walk along the pier as far as the lighthouse.

phrases.latin: Contracta piscēs aequora sentiunt jactīs in altum mōlibus
phrases.english: the fish feel the waters shrink as piers are thrown out into the deep

phrases.latin: Hujus sinistrum brachium firmissimō opere mūnītum est, dextrum ēlabōrātur.
phrases.english: Its left arm has been made fast with the strongest masonry; the right is being built.

sources: Lewis & Short: moles
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. breakwater.
